Discrete-Time Zero-Sum Markov Games with Control, Stopping, and State-Dependent Discounting
Guanghui Feng1  Xin Guo2,∗
1School of Mathematics, Sun Yat-sen University, China
2School of Science, Sun Yat-sen University, China

11footnotetext: Corresponding author at: School of Science, Sun Yat-sen University, 66 Gongchang Road, Guangming District, Shenzhen 518107, China. E-mail addresses: fenggh7@mail2.sysu.edu.cn (G. Feng), guox87@mail.sysu.edu.cn (X. Guo).
Abstract

We study a discrete-time two-player zero-sum stochastic game with control and stopping, where both players can stop the game, the discount factors depends on the states, and the running and terminal rewards may be unbounded. A contraction argument for the constrained Shapley equation establishes the existence of the value and a Nash equilibrium consisting of stationary controls and stopping times. We further provides algorithms for approximating the value and computing an ε\varepsilon-Nash equilibrium. A numerical example with state-dependent discount factors illustrates the results.

Keywords: zero-sum stochastic game; control and stopping; state-dependent discounting; unbounded payoff; constrained Shapley equation; value iteration; ε\varepsilon-Nash equilibrium.

1 Introduction

Dynamic game problems often involve both the operation of a system and the decision to terminate it. In an economic or operational relationship, the parties may adjust their actions while the system continues, but either party may also wish to end the relationship. Controls then determine the evolution of a state in the system, whereas stopping decisions determine how long rewards accumulate. The importance of future rewards may also vary with the current economic or operating state, motivating state-dependent discounting [21, 11]. For example, if a firm’s financing cost varies with its current cash reserves, the discount factor used to evaluate future returns may also depend on the current state. Moreover, rewards that grow with the size of the system need not be uniformly bounded. In a population model, for example, a total service cost proportional to the population size is unbounded when the population can take arbitrarily large integer values. These considerations lead to the problem studied here: a discrete-time zero-sum game in which both players control and stop, with state-dependent discount factors and possibly unbounded running and terminal rewards. For applications, we not only establish an equilibrium, but also give the algorithms to compute an ε\varepsilon-Nash equilibrium.

We first review related studies on stochastic games involving control, stopping, or both. In continuous time, stopping games allow players to choose when to stop a given process without controlling its dynamics [8, 7, 17]. When both players can control and stop, Pal and Saha [16] study a continuous-time Markov chain on a countable state space with a constant discount rate and possibly unbounded transition and reward rates. They establish the value and a saddle-point equilibrium. Related semi-Markov models also allow both players to control and stop. Bose, Pal, and Saha [2] consider a risk-sensitive discounted criterion in a semi-Markov setting and establish the value and a saddle-point equilibrium. In discrete time, classical stopping games, beginning with Dynkin [9], allow players to choose when to stop a given process without controlling its transition law. Subsequent studies establish value and equilibrium results under different reward assumptions and game structures [19, 20, 12]. A further class assigns control to one player and stopping to the other. Cavazos-Cadena and Hernández-Hernández [4] study such a game under an expected discounted criterion, establish the value and equilibria, and construct approximate equilibria through successive approximations. Under an expected total-reward criterion, equilibrium results are obtained under absorption conditions [5] or communication and ergodicity conditions [3]. More directly related to this paper are discrete-time games in which both players can control and stop. Ghosh and Mallikarjuna Rao [10] consider a Borel state space, constant discounting, bounded continuous rewards, and strictly ordered terminal rewards. They characterize the value by dynamic programming inequalities and establish a saddle-point equilibrium. In contrast, the present paper considers an expected discounted criterion with state-dependent discount factors and possibly unbounded running and terminal rewards.

State-dependent discounting has also been studied without this two-player control-and-stopping structure. For a single decision maker, Wei and Guo [21] allow unbounded rewards or costs, establish optimal stationary policies, and develop value iteration. Jasso-Fuentes, Menaldi, and Prieto-Rumeau [13] allow state-action-dependent discount factors, and characterize optimal policies and the value by dynamic programming; their framework includes control problems with stopping. For stochastic games without strategic stopping, Yu, Guo, and Xia [24] establish the value and optimal stationary strategies under an expected criterion with state-action-dependent discounting and weighted reward bounds, and develop an algorithm for the value and approximate equilibria in finite models. Guo, Chen, and Li [11] address discrete-time risk-sensitive games with varying discount factors and unbounded rewards under logarithmic growth conditions, and provide existence results and an iterative algorithm. These works supply important methods for variable discounting, but do not determine both players’ control policies and stopping times for the expected criterion studied here.

The gap addressed in this paper is the joint treatment of these decisions and reward conditions, together with an equilibrium computation algorithm. The expected-discounted control-and-stopping studies cited above use constant discount factors or rates, whereas the variable-discount control results concern a single decision maker or games without both players’ stopping decisions. These results do not directly give the existence and computation guarantees under the combined assumptions considered here. In discrete time, state-dependent discounting requires more than a notational replacement: the cumulative discount depends on the realized state path, whose distribution is affected by both controls. With unbounded rewards, one must control the discounted running rewards and the terminal rewards at random stopping times, and show how errors in the value approximation affect both controls and stopping decisions.

We establish the existence of the value and a Nash equilibrium on a countable state space under explicit reward-growth and transition conditions, with state-dependent discount factors uniformly bounded above by a constant less than one. First, a contraction argument in a weighted norm gives a unique solution of the constrained Shapley equation despite possibly unbounded rewards. Second, bounds for the cumulative discounts and terminal terms allow us to identify this solution with the value and construct a Nash equilibrium consisting of stationary controls and stopping times. These results treat state-dependent discounting under an expected criterion, in contrast to the constant-discount formulation in [10] and the risk-sensitive formulation in [25]. Third, following the contraction-based value-iteration method in Puterman [18, Sections 6.2.3 and 6.3.2], we obtain an error bound from successive terms of a single sequence. We first prove a weighted error bound and then, under the finiteness condition in Section 5, derive the uniform value-error bound needed for the Nash inequalities. The value-iteration principle is classical; its use here requires error bounds that account for both controls and stopping decisions under state-dependent discounting. For finite state and action spaces, the resulting algorithms compute the value approximation, both control policies, and both stopping sets by solving linear programs. Together, these results connect existence, value approximation, and equilibrium computation for a model combining both players’ control and stopping decisions with state-dependent discounting and possibly unbounded rewards. An infinite-state queueing example illustrates the computed strategies and the error guarantees.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 formulates the game and its criterion. Section 3 establishes the existence and uniqueness of the solution to the constrained Shapley equation. Section 4 proves the existence of the value and a Nash equilibrium. Section 5 develops the approximation procedures and algorithms, and Section 6 presents a numerical example.

Definition 2.1.

A strategy for player kk is a pair (πk,θk)(\pi^{k},\theta^{k}), where πk∈Πk\pi^{k}\in\Pi^{k} and θk∈Θ\theta^{k}\in\Theta.

Let D⊂XD\subset X be a prescribed set of states at which the system fails. Define the time of system failure by σD:=inf{t∈ℕ0:Xt∈D},\sigma_{D}:=\inf\{t\in\mathbb{N}_{0}:X_{t}\in D\}, where inf∅:=∞.\inf\varnothing:=\infty. Since

{σD≤t}=⋃s=0t{Xs∈D}∈𝒢t,t∈ℕ0,\{\sigma_{D}\leq t\}=\bigcup_{s=0}^{t}\{X_{s}\in D\}\in\mathcal{G}_{t},\qquad t\in\mathbb{N}_{0},

σD\sigma_{D} is a stopping time with respect to (𝒢t)(\mathcal{G}_{t}). Unlike the stopping times chosen by the players, σD\sigma_{D} is determined by the state process and the prescribed set DD.

The game proceeds as follows. Given stopping times θ1\theta^{1} and θ2\theta^{2} chosen by the two players, at each time tt, the players observe the current state xtx_{t} and the previously realized actions. If the current state belongs to DD, the game terminates immediately, with no additional terminal reward. Otherwise, the players independently decide whether to stop or continue. If both players continue, players 1 and 2 select at∈A⁡(xt)a_{t}\in A(x_{t}) and bt∈B⁡(xt)b_{t}\in B(x_{t}), respectively. Player 1 then receives the one-stage payoff r⁡(xt,at,bt)r(x_{t},a_{t},b_{t}) from player 2, and the state moves to xt+1∈Xx_{t+1}\in X according to p⁡(xt+1∣xt,at,bt)p(x_{t+1}\mid x_{t},a_{t},b_{t}). If player 1 stops at time tt before system failure and no later than player 2, player 1 receives the terminal reward g1​(xt)g_{1}(x_{t}). If player 2 stops at time tt before system failure and before player 1, player 1 receives the terminal reward g2​(xt)g_{2}(x_{t}). Thus all rewards in the criterion below are measured from player 1’s perspective. Player 1 seeks to maximize, and player 2 to minimize, the expected discounted criterion. The game terminates at θ1∧θ2∧σD\theta^{1}\wedge\theta^{2}\wedge\sigma_{D}. If system failure and a player’s stopping decision occur at the same time, the game terminates according to the system-failure rule. This procedure is repeated at each subsequent time until either player stops or the system fails.

Definition 2.2.

If J−​(x)=J+​(x)J^{-}(x)=J^{+}(x) for every x∈Dcx\in D^{c}, then their common function, denoted by JJ, is called the value of the game.

Definition 2.3.

Suppose that the game has a value JJ. A strategy (π∗1,θ∗1)(\pi^{1}_{*},\theta^{1}_{*}) is optimal for player 1 if

Remark.

State-dependent discounting with unbounded rewards has been studied for Markov decision processes in [21] and for semi-Markov games without stopping decisions in [24]. The new feature relative to these studies is the treatment of state-dependent discounting in a discrete-time two-player game in which both players can control and stop.

4 The existence of the value and equilibrium

This section proves the existence of the value and a Nash equilibrium. For (x,a,b)∈K(x,a,b)\in K, λ∈𝒫⁡(A⁡(x))\lambda\in\mathcal{P}(A(x)), μ∈𝒫⁡(B⁡(x))\mu\in\mathcal{P}(B(x)), and stationary policies πk∈Πsk\pi^{k}\in\Pi_{s}^{k} (k=1,2)(k=1,2), define

p(⋅|x,λ,μ):=∫A⁡(x)∫B⁡(x)p(⋅|x,a,b)μ(db)λ(da),r(x,λ,μ):=∫A⁡(x)∫B⁡(x)r(x,a,b)μ(db)λ(da),\displaystyle p(\cdot|x,\lambda,\mu):=\int_{A(x)}\int_{B(x)}p(\cdot|x,a,b)\mu(db)\lambda(da),\ \ r(x,\lambda,\mu):=\int_{A(x)}\int_{B(x)}r(x,a,b)\mu(db)\lambda(da),

Under Assumption 3.3, the functions p⁡(y∣x,λ,μ)p(y\mid x,\lambda,\mu), r⁡(x,λ,μ)r(x,\lambda,\mu), and ∑y∈XV0​(y)​p​(y∣x,λ,μ)\sum_{y\in X}V_{0}(y)p(y\mid x,\lambda,\mu) are continuous in (λ,μ)∈𝒫⁡(A⁡(x))×𝒫⁡(B⁡(x))(\lambda,\mu)\in\mathcal{P}(A(x))\times\mathcal{P}(B(x)).

From the notations above, together with (3.3)

𝕀α​u​(x):=supλ∈𝒫⁡(A⁡(x))infμ∈𝒫⁡(B⁡(x))[r⁡(x,λ,μ)+α⁡(x)​∑y∈Xu⁡(y)​p​(y|x,λ,μ)]∀x∈Dc.\mathbb{I}_{\alpha}u(x):=\sup_{\lambda\in\mathcal{P}(A(x))}\inf_{\mu\in\mathcal{P}(B(x))}\bigg[r(x,\lambda,\mu)+\alpha(x)\sum_{y\in X}u(y)p(y|x,\lambda,\mu)\bigg]\ \ \forall x\in D^{c}. (4.1)

We first derive three inequalities from (3.6) which are needed to prove Theorem 4.2 below.

Lemma 4.1.

Let u∗u^{*} be the solution of (3.6) in Theorem 3.4. Then the following statements hold.

  • (a)

    For every x∈Dcx\in D^{c} such that g1​(x)<u∗​(x)<g2​(x)g_{1}(x)<u^{*}(x)<g_{2}(x), one has u∗​(x)=𝕀α​u∗​(x)u^{*}(x)=\mathbb{I}_{\alpha}u^{*}(x);

  • (b)

    For every x∈Dcx\in D^{c} such that g1​(x)≤u∗​(x)<g2​(x)g_{1}(x)\leq u^{*}(x)<g_{2}(x), one has 𝕀α​u∗​(x)≤u∗​(x)\mathbb{I}_{\alpha}u^{*}(x)\leq u^{*}(x);

  • (c)

    For every x∈Dcx\in D^{c} such that g1​(x)<u∗​(x)≤g2​(x)g_{1}(x)<u^{*}(x)\leq g_{2}(x), one has u∗​(x)≤𝕀α​u∗​(x)u^{*}(x)\leq\mathbb{I}_{\alpha}u^{*}(x).

Proof.

Throughout this proof, x∈Dcx\in D^{c}.

  • (a)

    Suppose that g1​(x)<u∗​(x)<g2​(x)g_{1}(x)<u^{*}(x)<g_{2}(x). Since u∗​(x)>g1​(x)u^{*}(x)>g_{1}(x), (3.6) implies u∗​(x)=min⁡{𝕀α​u∗​(x),g2​(x)}.u^{*}(x)=\min\{\mathbb{I}_{\alpha}u^{*}(x),g_{2}(x)\}. Moreover, u∗​(x)<g2​(x)u^{*}(x)<g_{2}(x).   • (b)

    Suppose that g1​(x)≤u∗​(x)<g2​(x)g_{1}(x)\leq u^{*}(x)<g_{2}(x). If 𝕀α​u∗​(x)>u∗​(x)\mathbb{I}_{\alpha}u^{*}(x)>u^{*}(x), then min⁡{𝕀α​u∗​(x),g2​(x)}>u∗​(x)≥g1​(x).\min\{\mathbb{I}_{\alpha}u^{*}(x),g_{2}(x)\}>u^{*}(x)\geq g_{1}(x). It would follow from (3.6) that u∗​(x)>u∗​(x)u^{*}(x)>u^{*}(x), which is impossible. Therefore, 𝕀α​u∗​(x)≤u∗​(x).\mathbb{I}_{\alpha}u^{*}(x)\leq u^{*}(x).

  • (c)

    Suppose that g1​(x)<u∗​(x)≤g2​(x)g_{1}(x)<u^{*}(x)\leq g_{2}(x). It follows that g2​(x)>g1​(x)g_{2}(x)>g_{1}(x), together with (3.6) gives u∗​(x)=min⁡{𝕀α​u∗​(x),g2​(x)}.u^{*}(x)=\min\{\mathbb{I}_{\alpha}u^{*}(x),g_{2}(x)\}. Therefore, u∗​(x)≤𝕀α​u∗​(x).u^{*}(x)\leq\mathbb{I}_{\alpha}u^{*}(x).

∎

For u∗u^{*} satisfying (3.6), define

Define the corresponding stopping times by

θu∗1:=inf{t|Xt∈Du∗1};θu∗2:=inf{t|Xt∈Du∗2}.\theta^{1}_{u^{*}}:=\inf\{t|X_{t}\in D^{1}_{u^{*}}\};\ \ \ \ \ \theta^{2}_{u^{*}}:=\inf\{t|X_{t}\in D^{2}_{u^{*}}\}. (4.3)

{θu∗i≤n}=⋃t=0n{Xt∈Du∗i}∈𝒢n,i=1,2,\{\theta_{u^{*}}^{i}\leq n\}=\bigcup_{t=0}^{n}\{X_{t}\in D_{u^{*}}^{i}\}\in\mathcal{G}_{n},\qquad i=1,2,

By the measurable selection theorem in [14], selecting controls on DcD^{c} and extending them arbitrarily to DD, there exists a pair (πu∗1,πu∗2)∈Πs1×Πs2(\pi^{1}_{u^{*}},\pi^{2}_{u^{*}})\in\Pi_{s}^{1}\times\Pi_{s}^{2} such that

=supλ∈𝒫⁡(A⁡(x))[r⁡(x,λ,πu∗2)+α⁡(x)​∑y∈Xu∗​(y)​p​(y|x,λ,πu∗2)]\displaystyle=\sup_{\lambda\in\mathcal{P}(A(x))}\bigg[r(x,\lambda,\pi^{2}_{u^{*}})+\alpha(x)\sum_{y\in X}u^{*}(y)p(y|x,\lambda,\pi^{2}_{u^{*}})\bigg]
=infμ∈𝒫⁡(B⁡(x))[r⁡(x,πu∗1,μ)+α⁡(x)​∑y∈Xu∗​(y)​p​(y|x,πu∗1,μ)]∀x∈Dc.\displaystyle=\inf_{\mu\in\mathcal{P}(B(x))}\bigg[r(x,\pi^{1}_{u^{*}},\mu)+\alpha(x)\sum_{y\in X}u^{*}(y)p(y|x,\pi^{1}_{u^{*}},\mu)\bigg]\ \ \ \forall x\in D^{c}. (4.4)

The next theorem is the principal existence result of this section.

Theorem 4.2.

Under Assumptions 3.1 and 3.3, let u∗u^{*} be the solution of (3.6) given by Theorem 3.4, and let (πu∗1,θu∗1,πu∗2,θu∗2)(\pi^{1}_{u^{*}},\theta^{1}_{u^{*}};\pi^{2}_{u^{*}},\theta^{2}_{u^{*}}) be defined by (4.2)–(4.4). Then:

  • (a)

∎

Remark.

Theorem 4.2 combines assumptions that are treated separately in the related control-and-stopping literature. Compared with the [10], which assumes bounded rewards and strictly ordered terminal rewards in its main results and discusses an extension through weighted norms, this paper allows the discount factor to depend on the current state and gives explicit conditions for possibly unbounded running and terminal rewards. Compared with [6], the present model uses state-dependent discount factors rather than a constant discount rate and does not require bounded rewards.

5 Computation of the value and equilibrium

This section develops algorithms for approximating the value and constructing an ε\varepsilon-Nash equilibrium. We prove approximation of the value JJ using the sequence {u^n}\{\hat{u}_{n}\} defined in (3.5). Since u^n≤J\hat{u}_{n}\leq J, the approximation error at state xx after nn iterations is J​(x)−u^n​(x)J(x)-\hat{u}_{n}(x). We bound this error using the difference between two successive iterates. Finite action sets are assumed for the linear-programming computations, not for the error bounds.

5.1 Computation of the value

Theorems 3.4 and 4.2 show that {u^n}\{\hat{u}_{n}\} in (3.5) increases to the value JJ. Following the contraction argument and value-iteration method in Puterman [18, Sections 6.2.3 and 6.3.2], we use the contraction inequality (3.8) to bound the error from the difference u^n−u^n−1\hat{u}_{n}-\hat{u}_{n-1}. Set κ:=α¯​m<1\kappa:=\bar{\alpha}m<1, as in the proof of Theorem 3.4.

Theorem 5.1.

Under Assumptions 3.1 and 3.3, the sequence {u^n}\{\hat{u}_{n}\} in (3.5) has the following properties.

  • (a)

    J=u∗J=u^{*}, where u∗u^{*} is the fixed point of 𝕋α\mathbb{T}_{\alpha} in (3.4). For x∈Dcx\in D^{c} and n≥0n\geq 0,

    g1​(x)≤u^n​(x)≤u^n+1​(x)≤J⁡(x)≤max⁡{g1​(x),g2​(x)}.g_{1}(x)\leq\hat{u}_{n}(x)\leq\hat{u}_{n+1}(x)\leq J(x)\leq\max\{g_{1}(x),g_{2}(x)\}.

    Moreover, {u^n}\{\hat{u}_{n}\} converges to JJ in ∥⋅∥V0\lVert\cdot\rVert_{V_{0}}.

  • (b)

    For every n≥1n\geq 1,

    ∥J−u^n∥V0≤κ1−κ​∥u^n−u^n−1∥V0≤κn1−κ​∥u^1−u^0∥V0.\lVert J-\hat{u}_{n}\rVert_{V_{0}}\leq\frac{\kappa}{1-\kappa}\lVert\hat{u}_{n}-\hat{u}_{n-1}\rVert_{V_{0}}\leq\frac{\kappa^{n}}{1-\kappa}\lVert\hat{u}_{1}-\hat{u}_{0}\rVert_{V_{0}}. (5.1)
Proof.
  • (a)

    By Theorem 4.2, J=u∗J=u^{*}. Theorem 3.4 gives u^n​(x)≤u^n+1​(x)\hat{u}_{n}(x)\leq\hat{u}_{n+1}(x) and weighted-norm convergence of {u^n}\{\hat{u}_{n}\}. Since u^0≤J\hat{u}_{0}\leq J and 𝕋α​J=J\mathbb{T}_{\alpha}J=J, the monotonicity of 𝕋α\mathbb{T}_{\alpha} gives

    u^n≤u^n+1=𝕋αn+1​u^0≤𝕋αn+1​J=J.\hat{u}_{n}\leq\hat{u}_{n+1}=\mathbb{T}_{\alpha}^{n+1}\hat{u}_{0}\leq\mathbb{T}_{\alpha}^{n+1}J=J.

    By (3.5)–(3.6), we have g1​(x)≤u^n​(x)≤u^n+1​(x)≤J⁡(x)≤max⁡{g1​(x),g2​(x)}g_{1}(x)\leq\hat{u}_{n}(x)\leq\hat{u}_{n+1}(x)\leq J(x)\leq\max\{g_{1}(x),g_{2}(x)\} on DcD^{c}. This proves (a).

  • (b)

    The contraction property (3.8) and 𝕋α​J=J\mathbb{T}_{\alpha}J=J give (5.1). By part (a) and the definition of the weighted norm,

    0≤J⁡(x)−u^n​(x)≤κ1−κ​∥u^n−u^n−1∥V0​V0​(x),x∈Dc,n≥1.0\leq J(x)-\hat{u}_{n}(x)\leq\frac{\kappa}{1-\kappa}\lVert\hat{u}_{n}-\hat{u}_{n-1}\rVert_{V_{0}}V_{0}(x),\qquad x\in D^{c},\quad n\geq 1. (5.2)

∎

To compute u^n​(x)\hat{u}_{n}(x) for x∈Dcx\in D^{c}, it suffices to evaluate 𝕀α​u​(x)\mathbb{I}_{\alpha}u(x) with u=u^n−1u=\hat{u}_{n-1}. When the action sets are finite, this quantity is the value of a zero-sum matrix game and can be computed by linear programming.

The primal program is

max⁡v{v≤∑a∈A⁡(x)𝕀α​u​(x,a,b)​ϕ​(a),b∈B⁡(x)∑a∈A⁡(x)ϕ⁡(a)=1ϕ(a)≥0,a∈A(x),\begin{array}[]{rl}&\max v\\[3.0pt] &\left\{\begin{aligned} &v\leq\sum_{a\in A(x)}\mathbb{I}_{\alpha}u(x,a,b)\phi(a),\quad b\in B(x)\\ &\sum_{a\in A(x)}\phi(a)=1\\ &\phi(a)\geq 0,\,a\in A(x),\end{aligned}\right.\end{array} (5.3)

where 𝕀α​u​(x,a,b)\mathbb{I}_{\alpha}u(x,a,b) is defined as 𝕀α​u​(x,a,b):=r⁡(x,a,b)+α⁡(x)​∑y∈Xu⁡(y)​p​(y|x,a,b)\mathbb{I}_{\alpha}u(x,a,b):=r(x,a,b)+\alpha(x)\sum_{y\in X}u(y)p(y|x,a,b).

The dual program is

min⁡z{z≥∑b∈B⁡(x)𝕀α​u​(x,a,b)​ψ​(b),a∈A⁡(x)∑b∈B⁡(x)ψ⁡(b)=1ψ(b)≥0,b∈B(x).\begin{array}[]{rl}&\min z\\[3.0pt] &\left\{\begin{aligned} &z\geq\sum_{b\in B(x)}\mathbb{I}_{\alpha}u(x,a,b)\psi(b),\quad a\in A(x)\\ &\sum_{b\in B(x)}\psi(b)=1\\ &\psi(b)\geq 0,\,b\in B(x).\end{aligned}\right.\end{array} (5.4)

When A⁡(x)A(x) and B⁡(x)B(x) are finite, both programs admit solutions. Denote optimal solutions of (5.3) and (5.4) by ϕu(⋅∣x)\phi_{u}(\cdot\mid x) and ψu(⋅∣x)\psi_{u}(\cdot\mid x), respectively. They form a saddle point for the one-stage zero-sum game with payoff 𝕀α​u​(x,a,b)\mathbb{I}_{\alpha}u(x,a,b); see, for example, [1, Section 2.4]. Consequently,

Theorem 5.2(c) gives the following stopping rule, while Theorem 5.2(b) gives the corresponding error bound. A finite X∗X_{*} ensures that the rule is attained.

Algorithm I (Approximation of the value of the game):
Step 1 (Initialization): Input δ>0\delta>0, set n=0n=0, and take u^0\hat{u}_{0} from (3.5). Form the finite set X∗X_{*}. If X∗=∅X_{*}=\varnothing, return Jδ=u^0J_{\delta}=\hat{u}_{0}.

maxx∈X∗⁡|u^n​(x)−u^n−1​(x)|≤1−α¯α¯​δ,\max_{x\in X_{*}}|\hat{u}_{n}(x)-\hat{u}_{n-1}(x)|\leq\frac{1-\bar{\alpha}}{\bar{\alpha}}\delta,

go to Step 4. Otherwise, return to Step 2.

Step 4 (Value approximation): Return Jδ=u^nJ_{\delta}=\hat{u}_{n}. Then 0≤J⁡(x)−Jδ​(x)≤δ0\leq J(x)-J_{\delta}(x)\leq\delta for every x∈Dcx\in D^{c}.

The proof of Theorem 5.3 leads to the following algorithm.

Algorithm II (Computation of an ε\varepsilon-Nash equilibrium):
Step 1 (Initialization): Input an accuracy ε>0\varepsilon>0, set δε:=α¯​(1−α¯)​ε6\delta_{\varepsilon}:=\frac{\bar{\alpha}(1-\bar{\alpha})\varepsilon}{6}, and run Algorithm I with accuracy δε\delta_{\varepsilon} to obtain JδεJ_{\delta_{\varepsilon}} satisfying (5.8).
Step 2 (Stopping sets): Construct Dε1:={x∈Dc:g1​(x)−Jδε​(x)≥−ε4}D_{\varepsilon}^{1}:=\{x\in D^{c}:g_{1}(x)-J_{\delta_{\varepsilon}}(x)\geq-\frac{\varepsilon}{4}\} and Dε2:={x∈Dc:g2​(x)−Jδε​(x)≤ε4}D_{\varepsilon}^{2}:=\{x\in D^{c}:g_{2}(x)-J_{\delta_{\varepsilon}}(x)\leq\frac{\varepsilon}{4}\}.
Step 3 (ε\varepsilon-optimal policies): Choose arbitrary admissible stationary controls on DD. For each x∈Dcx\in D^{c}, solve (5.3) and (5.4) with u​(x):=Jδε​(x)u(x):=J_{\delta_{\varepsilon}}(x) to obtain πε1(⋅∣x)\pi_{\varepsilon}^{1}(\cdot\mid x) and πε2(⋅∣x)\pi_{\varepsilon}^{2}(\cdot\mid x).
Step 4 (ε\varepsilon-optimal stopping): Define θε1:=inf{t≥0:Xt∈Dε1}\theta_{\varepsilon}^{1}:=\inf\{t\geq 0:X_{t}\in D_{\varepsilon}^{1}\} and θε2:=inf{t≥0:Xt∈Dε2}\theta_{\varepsilon}^{2}:=\inf\{t\geq 0:X_{t}\in D_{\varepsilon}^{2}\}. System failure terminates the game at σD\sigma_{D} regardless of these stopping decisions. Then (πε1,θε1,πε2,θε2)(\pi_{\varepsilon}^{1},\theta_{\varepsilon}^{1};\pi_{\varepsilon}^{2},\theta_{\varepsilon}^{2}) is an ε\varepsilon-Nash equilibrium.

Corollary 5.4.

If XX, A⁡(x)A(x), and B⁡(x)B(x) are finite, then, for every ε>0\varepsilon>0, Algorithms I and II produce an ε\varepsilon-Nash equilibrium (πε1,θε1,πε2,θε2)(\pi_{\varepsilon}^{1},\theta_{\varepsilon}^{1};\pi_{\varepsilon}^{2},\theta_{\varepsilon}^{2}).

Remark.

Ghosh and Mallikarjuna Rao [10] characterize exact equilibria through the value equation but do not provide a numerical procedure with a prescribed equilibrium accuracy. In the present model, Theorem 5.2 gives, for finite X∗X_{*} and n≥1n\geq 1,

0≤J⁡(x)−u^n​(x)≤α¯1−α¯​maxy∈X∗​|u^n​(y)−u^n−1​(y)|.0\leq J(x)-\hat{u}_{n}(x)\leq\frac{\bar{\alpha}}{1-\bar{\alpha}}\max_{y\in X_{*}}|\hat{u}_{n}(y)-\hat{u}_{n-1}(y)|.

The contraction-based value-iteration principle is classical. Here its error bound is linked, through the choice of δε\delta_{\varepsilon}, to both players’ stationary controls and stopping times with an ε\varepsilon-Nash guarantee. For finite state and action spaces, the procedure uses linear programs with the state-dependent discount factors and updates only one value sequence.

6 A queueing game with unbounded rewards

This section considers a service queue. We first specify the model and verify the conditions for the existence of the value and a Nash equilibrium. We then choose numerical parameters to illustrate the computation of the value and an ε\varepsilon-Nash equilibrium.

Consider a client who submits tasks to a service provider under an agreement with service charges, compensation for unfinished tasks, and termination payments. The client is player 1, and the provider is player 2. There is no upper bound on the number of unfinished tasks, including any task being processed. If xx is the number of unfinished tasks, the state space is X:={0,1,2,…}X:=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}. A positive reward is a payment from the provider to the client, and a negative reward is a payment in the opposite direction. Thus, the client maximizes the expected discounted criterion in (2.6), whereas the provider minimizes the same criterion. Either party may terminate the agreement. We take D=∅D=\varnothing, so termination is determined by their stopping decisions rather than system failure.

At each decision epoch when both parties continue, the client chooses whether to increase its submission frequency: a=0a=0 means normal submission, and a=1a=1 means increased submission. The provider chooses whether to allocate additional processing capacity: b=0b=0 means normal processing, and b=1b=1 means additional processing capacity. Thus, A⁡(x)=B⁡(x):={0,1}A(x)=B(x):=\{0,1\} for every x∈Xx\in X. We assume that at most one task is submitted and at most one task is completed during each period, and that submission and completion do not occur in the same period. Given actions aa and bb, a new task is submitted and admitted with probability q+​(a)q^{+}(a). If x>0x>0, one task is completed with probability q−​(b)q^{-}(b). If x=0x=0, no task can be completed. Assume that

0≤q+​(0)<q+​(1),0≤q−​(0)<q−​(1),q+​(1)+q−​(1)≤1.0\leq q^{+}(0)<q^{+}(1),\qquad 0\leq q^{-}(0)<q^{-}(1),\qquad q^{+}(1)+q^{-}(1)\leq 1.

Thus, for x≥1x\geq 1, the queue length increases by one with probability q+​(a)q^{+}(a), decreases by one with probability q−​(b)q^{-}(b), and remains unchanged with probability 1−q+​(a)−q−​(b)1-q^{+}(a)-q^{-}(b). Consequently, the transition probabilities are

p⁡(y∣x,a,b)=\displaystyle p(y\mid x,a,b)={} q+(a)I{y=x+1}+q−(b)I{y=max{x−1,0}}+(1−q+(a)−q−(b))I{y=x}.\displaystyle q^{+}(a)I_{\{y=x+1\}}+q^{-}(b)I_{\{y=\max\{x-1,0\}\}}+\bigl(1-q^{+}(a)-q^{-}(b)\bigr)I_{\{y=x\}}. (6.1)

At the empty state, (6.1) gives

p⁡(1∣0,a,b)=q+​(a),p⁡(0∣0,a,b)=1−q+​(a).p(1\mid 0,a,b)=q^{+}(a),\qquad p(0\mid 0,a,b)=1-q^{+}(a).

Let c,ca,cbc,c_{a},c_{b} be nonnegative constants and h>0h>0. In each period of continued operation, the client pays a basic service charge cc and receives compensation hh per unfinished task. The client also pays an additional submission fee cac_{a} if a=1a=1 and an additional service fee cbc_{b} if b=1b=1. These are payments between the two parties; external operating costs are not included in the criterion. The resulting one-stage reward to the client is

r⁡(x,a,b):=−c+h​x−ca​a−cb​b.r(x,a,b):=-c+hx-c_{a}a-c_{b}b. (6.2)

Let η,ζ,k1\eta,\zeta,k_{1} be nonnegative constants and k2>0k_{2}>0, describing the termination payments. The agreement specifies an integer N≥1N\geq 1: when fewer than NN tasks remain and the client terminates the agreement, a fixed charge η\eta is reduced by a refund k1k_{1} per unfinished task. If the provider terminates it first, the client receives compensation ζ\zeta plus k2k_{2} per unfinished task. When at least NN tasks remain, the client receives this latter compensation regardless of which party terminates the agreement. Thus NN specifies when the common termination payment applies; it is not a capacity limit. The terminal payoff functions are

g1​(x):={−η+k1​x,0≤x<N,ζ+k2​x,x≥N,g2​(x):=ζ+k2​x.g_{1}(x):=\begin{cases}-\eta+k_{1}x,&0\leq x<N,\\ \zeta+k_{2}x,&x\geq N,\end{cases}\qquad g_{2}(x):=\zeta+k_{2}x. (6.3)

As in (2.6), g1g_{1} applies when player 1 stops no later than player 2, and g2g_{2} applies when player 2 stops first. All rewards are measured from the client’s perspective. No ordering between g1g_{1} and g2g_{2} is imposed for x<Nx<N. For x≥Nx\geq N, the two termination payments agree. Since h,k2>0h,k_{2}>0, the running reward and both terminal rewards tend to +∞+\infty as x→∞x\to\infty.

Both parties evaluate future net payments using a common discount factor α⁡(x)∈(0,1)\alpha(x)\in(0,1) at state xx. Assume that α¯=supx∈Xα⁡(x)<1\bar{\alpha}=\sup_{x\in X}\alpha(x)<1. The cumulative discount is the product of these factors along the state path, as in (2.6).

Proposition 6.1.

Under the conditions specified above, the model in (6.1)–(6.3) satisfies Assumptions 3.1 and 3.3 with V0​(x)=ℓ+xV_{0}(x)=\ell+x for a sufficiently large constant ℓ≥1\ell\geq 1. The value and a Nash equilibrium exist, and Algorithms I and II apply.

The conditions on q+q^{+} and q−q^{-} give 0≤q+​(a)+q−​(b)≤10\leq q^{+}(a)+q^{-}(b)\leq 1 for every (a,b)(a,b). Hence (6.1) defines a transition probability distribution on XX. ∑y∈XV0(y)p(y∣x,a,b)=V0(x)+q+(a)−q−(b)I{x≥1}≤V0(x)+q+(1)≤(1+q+​(1)ℓ)V0(x).\displaystyle\sum_{y\in X}V_{0}(y)p(y\mid x,a,b)=V_{0}(x)+q^{+}(a)-q^{-}(b)I_{\{x\geq 1\}}\leq V_{0}(x)+q^{+}(1)\leq\left(1+\frac{q^{+}(1)}{\ell}\right)V_{0}(x).

This proves (3.1) with m=1+q+​(1)ℓm=1+\frac{q^{+}(1)}{\ell} and α¯​m<1\bar{\alpha}m<1. Set

c0:=max⁡{c+ca+cbℓ,h,ηℓ,k1,ζℓ,k2}.c_{0}:=\max\left\{\frac{c+c_{a}+c_{b}}{\ell},h,\frac{\eta}{\ell},k_{1},\frac{\zeta}{\ell},k_{2}\right\}.

By (6.2)–(6.3), for every (x,a,b)(x,a,b),

|r⁡(x,a,b)|\displaystyle|r(x,a,b)| ≤c+ca+cb+h​x≤c0​V0​(x),\displaystyle\leq c+c_{a}+c_{b}+hx\leq c_{0}V_{0}(x),
|g1​(x)|\displaystyle|g_{1}(x)| ≤max⁡{η+k1​x,ζ+k2​x}≤c0​V0​(x),\displaystyle\leq\max\{\eta+k_{1}x,\zeta+k_{2}x\}\leq c_{0}V_{0}(x),
|g2​(x)|\displaystyle|g_{2}(x)| =ζ+k2​x≤c0​V0​(x).\displaystyle=\zeta+k_{2}x\leq c_{0}V_{0}(x).

Thus Assumption 3.1 holds. Finiteness of the action sets gives compactness and the continuity required in Assumption 3.3. Moreover,

X∗:={x∈X:g1​(x)≠g2​(x)}⊆{0,1,…,N−1},X_{*}:=\{x\in X:g_{1}(x)\neq g_{2}(x)\}\subseteq\{0,1,\ldots,N-1\},

so X∗X_{*} is finite. Theorem 4.2 and Theorems 5.2–5.3 give the stated conclusions. In particular,

u^n​(x)=J⁡(x)=ζ+k2​x,x≥N,n≥0.\hat{u}_{n}(x)=J(x)=\zeta+k_{2}x,\qquad x\geq N,\quad n\geq 0.

∎

In this model, rr, g1g_{1}, and g2g_{2} are unbounded, unlike the bounded-reward assumptions in the main results of Ghosh and Mallikarjuna Rao [10], which also use a constant discount factor. Pal and Saha [16] give a continuous-time queueing example with a constant discount rate. Here, the decisions are made in discrete time and the discount factor depends on the current queue length. The common termination payment for x≥Nx\geq N makes X∗X_{*} finite without bounding the rewards.
